newsitem.title: USA: Lung Association urges stronger air standards.
newsitem.headline: Lung Association urges stronger air standards.

text.p: The American Lung Association Monday said the Clinton administration's proposal to strengthen air quality standards would leave 89 million people potentially exposed to dangerous air pollution levels.

"We strongly support EPA's (Environmental Protection Agency) effort to set standards that would be more protective of public health. But we believe EPA can and must do even better," Alfred Munzer, past president of the American Lung Association, said at a news conference.

The association said the EPA's proposed stricter standard on soot and dust pollution, which for the first time would target the tiniest particles that may lodge deep in lungs, would not adequately protect those most vulnerable to lung ailments.

Among the 89 million people exposed to unsafe levels of particulate pollution under the EPA plan, it said, were 16.9 million children, 11.8 million elderly, 5 million asthmatics, 5 million people with chronic obstructive lung disease and 2.9 million people with coronary heart disease.

Instead of the EPA's proposed standard for the tiniest particles that would allow 50 micrograms per cubic meter of air measured over a 24-hour period, the Lung Association advocated a limit of 18 micrograms per cubic meter.

The current standard is geared more toward larger dust and soot particles, which experts said did not pose as great a health threat because the respiratory system screened them out before they reached the lungs.
The EPA has estimated its proposed standards, which also would tighten the larger particle limit, would prevent 20,000 premature deaths annually from air particle pollution.

But some industries argue that the nation has made huge strides in cleaning the air and standards do not need to be changed. They also contend that meeting stricter standards, including another EPA proposal to set a tighter rule against smog pollution, would impose huge economic costs.
